message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for drawing pixels on screen, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few cores (typically 2–32 in consumer CPUs). | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores (e.g., 2,000+ in modern GPUs). |
| **Core design** | Complex, high‑performance cores with deep pipelines, large caches, branch prediction, etc. | Simpler, lightweight cores optimized for throughput rather than single‑thread latency. |
| **Instruction set** | Rich, complex instruction sets (x86, ARM) with many features for control flow, memory management, etc. | Often a subset of the CPU’s ISA, focused on SIMD (single‑instruction, multiple data) operations. |
| **Execution model** | Mostly serial or lightly parallel; each core can run a few threads concurrently. | Highly parallel: thousands of threads execute the same instruction stream simultaneously (SIMT). |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated cache coherence protocols. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on fast shared memory (VRAM) and high bandwidth bus. |
| **Typical workloads** | Single‑threaded performance, branching code, I/O, OS kernel, database queries, web servers. | Data‑parallel tasks: image/video processing, machine learning inference/training, scientific simulations, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Power & heat** | Designed for low power consumption per core; thermal limits are tighter. | Can consume more power overall due to many cores, but each core is low‑power; GPUs often have higher TDPs. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional CPU programming (C/C++, Java, etc.) with multi‑threading libraries. | Requires specialized APIs (CUDA, OpenCL, DirectX, Vulkan) or frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch) that expose parallelism. |

### Why the difference matters

- **Latency vs Throughput**: CPUs excel at low‑latency, single‑thread performance. GPUs excel at high throughput for many independent operations.
- **Branching**: CPUs handle divergent branches efficiently; GPUs suffer when threads diverge because they execute in lockstep.
- **Memory access patterns**: GPUs benefit from coalesced memory accesses; CPUs can handle irregular patterns better.

In practice, most modern systems use both: the CPU handles general tasks and orchestrates work, while the GPU accelerates specific compute‑heavy or graphics‑heavy parts. This hybrid approach is common in gaming PCs, data centers, and AI research labs.
